ai.subject: Physiology
ai.summary: Cl‑cotransporters move chloride together with another ion (Na⁺ or K⁺) across cell membranes, crucial for renal salt handling and neuronal excitability. Dysfunction causes electrolyte disorders and hypertension.

sections.p: Cl‑cotransporters are membrane proteins that couple the movement of Cl⁻ with Na⁺ (NCC) or Na⁺/K⁺ (NKCC) without using ATP. They maintain cell volume, set intracellular Cl⁻, and drive Na⁺ reabsorption in the kidney.
b: Located in renal tubules, inner ear, brain, and vascular smooth muscle
Part of the SLC12 solute carrier family

sections.p: In the distal convoluted tubule (DCT), NCC reabsorbs Na⁺ and Cl⁻ from the lumen into the cell, driven by the Na⁺ gradient created by the basolateral Na⁺/K⁺‑ATPase. NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb works similarly but also brings K⁺.
b: NKCC2: 1 Na⁺ + 1 K⁺ + 2 Cl⁻ per cycle

sections.p: Phosphorylation by the WNK‑SPAK/OSR1 kinase cascade increases transporter activity; hormones (aldosterone, vasopressin) modulate expression; intracellular Cl⁻ concentration provides feedback inhibition.
b: Low intracellular Cl⁻ → WNK activation → ↑ NCC/NKCC activity

sections.p: Genetic or acquired defects alter NaCl reabsorption, leading to electrolyte imbalance, blood pressure changes, or neurologic symptoms.
b: Gitelman syndrome – loss‑of‑function NCC → hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, hypomagnesemia
Bartter syndrome type I – NKCC2 loss → salt wasting, polyuria, hypercalciuria

sections.p: Understanding Cl‑cotransporters guides diuretic choice, explains inherited tubulopathies, and informs treatment of hypertension and edema.
b: Thiazides treat hypertension by blocking NCC
Loop diuretics block NKCC2, useful in CHF and AKI

t.b: What is the pattern of Na⁺, K⁺, Cl⁻, Mg²⁺? → Detects Gitelman vs. Bartter vs. diuretic effect
Is calcium loss high? → Hypercalciuria suggests NKCC2 loss (Bartter) or loop diuretic use
Is hypertension present? → Suggests secondary NCC activation (e.g., hyperaldosteronism)

sections.p: Focus on distinguishing Gitelman from Bartter, the mechanism of thiazide and loop diuretics, and the regulatory kinase pathway.
b: Gitelman = NCC defect → low Mg²⁺, normal Ca²⁺
Bartter = NKCC2 defect → high Ca²⁺ loss

whenToSeekHelp: Severe hypokalemia (<2.5 mmol/L) with muscle weakness or arrhythmia
Unexplained refractory hypertension in a young adult
Acute volume depletion with hypotension after diuretic use

faq.a: Blocking NCC increases Na⁺ delivery to the collecting duct, enhancing Na⁺ reabsorption via ENaC and driving K⁺ secretion.

faq.q: How does NKCC2 inhibition lead to calcium stones?
faq.a: Less positive lumen voltage reduces paracellular Ca²⁺ reabsorption, increasing urinary calcium.

faq.q: Can Gitelman syndrome be confused with chronic thiazide use?
faq.a: Yes; both show similar labs, but Gitelman is lifelong, often with low Mg²⁺ and no diuretic exposure.

exam: Explain how thiazide diuretics lower blood pressure at the molecular level.
Compare the electrolyte patterns of Gitelman and Bartter syndromes and the underlying transporter defects.
Describe the WNK‑SPAK pathway’s role in regulating NCC activity.
